CBD, told out of order¶

a highlight reel — a decade of CBD discourse (2011–2021), 3.46M tweets read against the FDA's own record¶

We open at the end.

⏱ Cold open — same window, opposite fate¶

Two CBD health claims were born the same year (2013), in the same words. One — CBD cures cancer — drew FDA warning letters. The other — CBD stops seizures — became an FDA-approved medicine (Epidiolex, 2018). At the moment they emerged, nothing in the language told them apart.

That's the ending. Here's how we got there — and why it means a monitor can map the shape of a discourse but must never be trusted to call the truth.

① The word was a lie before the drug was¶

Rewind. For the first half of the decade, most “CBD” on Twitter wasn't the compound at all — it was the Central Business District (Sydney, Cape Town, downtown). The cannabidiol sense only took over around 2015. Miss this polysemy and every later number is contaminated; the whole study rests on separating the two senses first.

Validation. A strongly negative Spearman rho (close to −1) quantifies the monotone decline; a Kleinberg dominance window concentrated in the early 2010s, followed by collapse to near-zero rates by 2019-2021, confirms the district sense yielded the corpus. The §6 cannabidiol-commerce burst (2016Q4-2019Q4) and the district dominance window should be disjoint — the sense transition.

Falsifier. A flat or rising district-marker rate, or a dominance window that extends into 2018+, would mean the district sense did not collapse — contradicting both § 4 keyness (where the district terms are heavily early-distinctive) and the semantic-shift narrative.

② We could see the reframing coming¶

As cannabidiol took over, the talk medicalized — and it did so years before regulators moved. (Descriptive lead, not a claim we could have prevented anything.)

Not one disease at a time — a whole cascade of medical claims, most emerging before the 2019 FDA enforcement wave:

③ The claims — and the regulator's receipts¶

We turned the FDA's own warning letters into ground truth: 1,602 quoted claims from 130 letters (2015–2025). The result, replicating prior infodemiology work: 41% of CBD tweets echo a flagged claim — 8× more than medical text that isn't about CBD. (“Echo” = resemblance to a flagged claim — promoters and debunkers alike — never a verdict of falsity.)

Resolved by medical term — public discourse vs. regulatory enforcement, side by side:

④ The COVID dress rehearsal¶

When COVID-19 hit, the whole pattern ran in fast-forward: a cannabidiol-COVID surge that crested ~5 weeks before the FDA's first warning letters (Mar 28, 2020).

⑤ How we did it without fooling ourselves¶

The reveal saved for last: the machinery. Distinctive-term keyness caught the district → cannabidiol → health shift; a sense-drift monitor (borrowed from streaming concept-drift detection) timed when and how the meaning changed; and every headline survived an audit — label-shuffle nulls, placebo intervention dates, bootstrap confidence intervals, and the polysemy safeguard above.

⑥ The takeaway — quantify, don't adjudicate¶

A monitor can tell you when and how a health sub-discourse emerges, with years of lead time and falsifiable, volume-controlled measures. It cannot tell you whether the claims are true — because truth moves (epilepsy: flagged → approved) and is fused at emergence (cancer and epilepsy, same year, same words). Use these tools for early warning and human review — never for an automated verdict.

This is a curated cut. The full, reproducible notebook — every figure plus the complete audit layer — is the source of truth: cbd_case_study.
